explanation: Verses 7–12 record that this happened because the people of Israel sinned against the LORD, feared other gods, followed the customs of the nations that the LORD had driven out before them, set up pillars, and served idols. The option about Assyria being militarily stronger is merely an outward military cause, not the spiritual reason the author emphasizes (true_but_off). Refusing to pay tribute is the political trigger for Hoshea's arrest (v. 4), not the spiritual cause of the exile (near_passage). Allying with Egypt is one specific action, but the text assigns the core guilt to idol worship rather than to the choice of ally (wrong_scope).

content: Why did the king of Assyria have to send a priest back to teach the newly settled people of Samaria the law of the LORD?
options: Because the new settlers did not fear the LORD and were being killed by lions, the king assumed it was because they did not know the regulations of the god of that land
Because the new settlers immediately wanted to convert fully and voluntarily asked to be taught how to worship the LORD
Because the LORD himself appeared and commanded the king of Assyria to send a priest there to instruct the people
Because the remaining Israelites in the land revolted, demanding that the king restore their former worship
explanation: Verses 24–26 record that the king brought people from Babylon and various lands to settle in Samaria; at first they did not fear the LORD, so the LORD sent lions among them which killed some of them. People reported to the king that these nations did not know the law of the god of that land, so the king commanded that one of the exiled priests be brought back to teach them (vv. 27–28). The option of the people willingly converting is wrong: the motivation was fear of lions and a misunderstanding about the local deity, not genuine devotion (common_misconception). The LORD appearing directly to command the king of Assyria is a fabricated detail; the initiative came from the report that people brought to the king (wrong_detail). The remaining Israelites revolting is wrong because they had already been deported; the people in view here were the newly arrived foreigners (wrong_scope).

content: What characteristic of the worship practiced by the newly settled foreigners in Samaria made it displeasing to the LORD?
options: They both feared the LORD and served their own gods according to the customs of their homelands
They completely rejected the LORD and worshiped only their foreign gods
They worshiped the LORD fully but offered sacrifices in the wrong manner
They built a proper temple for the LORD in Jerusalem but abandoned Samaria
explanation: Verses 33 and 41 record that these nations feared the LORD but at the same time served their own gods according to the customs of the peoples from whom they had been carried away; this was syncretistic worship that violated the covenant requiring exclusive devotion to the LORD (vv. 35–39). The option of completely rejecting the LORD is wrong in one detail: the text says they still feared the LORD—the problem was mixture, not outright rejection (wrong_detail). Worshiping the LORD fully but offering sacrifices incorrectly is wrong because the core fault was worshiping additional gods, not the manner of sacrifice (common_misconception). Building a proper temple in Jerusalem is a fabricated detail outside the text, which concerns the people of Samaria, not Jerusalem (wrong_scope).

content: How old was Hezekiah when he began to reign over Judah?
options: Twenty-five years old
Twenty-nine years old
Twelve years old
Thirty-two years old
explanation: 2 Kings 18:2 states: 'Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem.' (B) Twenty-nine is the number of YEARS he reigned, not the age at which he became king (wrong_detail). (C) Twelve was the age at which Manasseh, Hezekiah's son, became king, mentioned later in the text (wrong_scope). (D) Thirty-two is a fabricated number with no connection to any milestone in the text (wrong_detail).

content: Hezekiah broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made; what name did he give it?
options: Asherah
Nehushtan
Baal
Dagon
explanation: 2 Kings 18:4 records that Hezekiah 'broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made... He called it Nehushtan.' (A) Asherah refers to the sacred poles he also cut down, but it was not the name given to the bronze serpent (near_passage). (C) Baal was a deity of the surrounding nations and does not appear in this verse (wrong_scope). (D) Dagon was the god of the Philistines, entirely outside the scope of this passage (wrong_scope).

content: When Hezekiah heard the threats from Assyria, which prophet did he send to inquire of?
options: The prophet Elijah
The prophet Elisha
The prophet Isaiah
The prophet Jeremiah
explanation: 2 Kings 19:2 records that Hezekiah sent his officials to 'Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz.' (A) Elijah was a prophet during the reign of King Ahab, much earlier in history (wrong_scope). (B) Elisha was the prophet who succeeded Elijah and had already died before Hezekiah's time (near_passage). (D) Jeremiah ministered later, during the reigns of the last kings of Judah (wrong_scope).

content: After his defeat and return, where was the Assyrian king Sennacherib killed?
options: In the city of Nineveh
In the city of Lachish
In the city of Samaria
In the land of Ararat
explanation: 2 Kings 19:36-37 records that Sennacherib withdrew and 'lived at Nineveh,' and while he was worshiping in the house of his god Nisroch, his two sons struck him down with the sword. (B) Lachish was where he had been encamped while besieging Judah, not where he died (near_passage). (C) Samaria was where Assyria had previously conquered; this confuses the location (wrong_detail). (D) The land of Ararat was where his two sons fled after killing their father — not where Sennacherib himself died (near_passage).

content: To persuade Sennacherib to withdraw his troops, Hezekiah paid tribute — and to raise enough gold he had to do something extraordinary. What was it?
options: Take gold from the royal treasury
Strip the gold from the doors and pillars of the temple
Collect gold from the people of the city
Borrow gold from the king of Egypt
explanation: 2 Kings 18:15-16 records that Hezekiah gave all the silver in the temple and in the king's treasury, and then 'stripped the gold from the doors of the temple of the LORD and from the doorposts' to give to the king of Assyria. (A) The royal treasury supplied only silver alongside the temple treasury; the gold itself had to be stripped from the temple doors — this answer is partially correct and therefore easy to confuse (near_passage). (C) Collecting gold from the people of the city is not mentioned anywhere in the text (wrong_detail). (D) Borrowing gold from the king of Egypt is what the Rabshakeh mocked as Hezekiah's vain reliance on Egypt; Hezekiah did not actually do this to pay the tribute (common_misconception).

content: Rabshakeh compared Judah's reliance on Egypt to leaning on what object?
options: A cracked wall about to collapse
A crushed reed that pierces the hand
A rotting rope easily broken
A leaking boat
explanation: 2 Kings 18:21 records Rabshakeh saying Egypt is 'that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it.' The image emphasizes that relying on Egypt is both useless and harmful. (A) A cracked wall about to collapse suggests collapse but is not the image in the text (wrong_detail). (C) A rotting rope conveys fragility but the detail differs from 'a crushed reed' (wrong_detail). (D) A leaking boat is also a metaphor for uselessness but does not appear in this passage (wrong_detail).

content: Why did Hezekiah's officials ask Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic instead of the language of Judah, and how did he respond?
options: To discuss matters secretly, but he refused to speak Aramaic
So the people on the wall would not understand, but he deliberately spoke in the language of Judah at full volume
To show respect for the king of Assyria, so he agreed
To avoid offending God, but he mocked them
explanation: 2 Kings 18:26-28 records that the officials asked him to speak in Aramaic 'for the people on the wall are listening,' but Rabshakeh deliberately 'stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah' so that the people would hear the threats and be terrified. (A) Wrong because the reason was not to discuss secrets but to keep the words from the people (wrong_detail), and the account of his response is also wrong. (C) The purpose was not to show respect, and he did not agree (wrong_detail). (D) The reason had nothing to do with offending God, and the text does not say he laughed at that (wrong_detail).

content: When Hezekiah received Sennacherib's threatening letter, what did he do in response?
options: Summoned his army to prepare for battle
Spread the letter out before the LORD and prayed
Sent additional tribute to seek peace with Assyria
Sent messengers to Egypt to request military reinforcements
explanation: 2 Kings 19:14-15 records that Hezekiah received the letter, 'went up to the house of the LORD and spread it before the LORD' and then prayed, asking to be delivered so that all nations would know that he alone is God. (A) The text emphasizes that he prayed rather than mobilized troops (wrong_detail). (C) He had previously paid tribute (18:14), but this time he did not seek peace — he turned to the LORD (true_but_off). (D) Relying on Egypt was what Rabshakeh had ridiculed; it was not what Hezekiah did on this occasion (common_misconception).

content: What news caused Sennacherib to send messengers with another threatening letter to Hezekiah instead of withdrawing?
options: News that Tirhakah king of Cush was marching out to fight him
News that the people of Judah had revolted against Assyrian rule
News that a rebellion had broken out inside Assyria
News that Hezekiah had formed an alliance with the king of Babylon
explanation: 2 Kings 19:8-9 records that Sennacherib heard that 'Tirhakah king of Cush had set out to fight against him'; this military threat caused him to quickly send messengers to pressure Hezekiah to surrender before he had to face two fronts. (B) Judah had indeed resisted Assyrian rule (18:7), but that is not the news that prompted him to send the letter at this moment (true_but_off). (C) Internal rebellion in Assyria occurred later and led to his death (19:37); it was not the reason here (wrong_scope). (D) The alliance with Babylon belongs to a different later episode involving the messengers of Merodach-baladan (wrong_scope).

content: In Isaiah's prophecy against Sennacherib, what did the LORD declare he would do to force this arrogant king to turn back?
options: Send an angel ahead to clear a safe path for his retreat
Put a hook in his nose and a bit in his mouth and turn him back the way he came
Send a plague upon his camp that would force him to withdraw
Fill his heart with fear so that he would order a retreat of his own accord
explanation: 2 Kings 19:28 records the LORD declaring that because of Sennacherib's arrogance, 'I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came.' The image of a hook — as used with an animal — emphasizes humiliation and the LORD's absolute sovereignty. (A) Wrong because the LORD did not clear a safe path but forced him to return in disgrace (wrong_detail). (C) The Assyrian camp was indeed struck by the angel of the LORD, resulting in the death of 185,000 soldiers (19:35), but that event is not the image presented in this prophecy (true_but_off). (D) The prophecy uses the image of a hook and bit controlled directly by the LORD himself, not the king retreating out of his own fear (wrong_detail).

content: What did the prophet Isaiah tell them to apply to King Hezekiah's boil so that the king would be healed?
options: A cake of figs
A handful of olive leaves
Some fragrant oil
A piece of linen cloth
explanation: 2 Kings 20:7 records that Isaiah said, 'Bring a cake of figs,' and they laid it on the boil, and the king recovered. Olive leaves (wrong_detail) do not appear in this passage. Fragrant oil (common_misconception) is confused with the anointing for healing found elsewhere in Scripture. Linen cloth (wrong_detail) is not the item applied to the boil.

content: The king of which country sent messengers with a letter and a gift to visit King Hezekiah when he heard that the king had been ill?
options: The king of Assyria
The king of Babylon
The king of Egypt
The king of Syria
explanation: 2 Kings 20:12 records that Berodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with a letter and a present because he heard that Hezekiah had been sick. Assyria (near_passage) was the enemy that besieged Jerusalem in chapters 18–19 but did not send a goodwill gift. Egypt (wrong_scope) was a nation Judah had relied upon but is not connected to this passage. Syria (wrong_detail) belongs to earlier battles in 2 Kings.

content: How many years did King Manasseh reign in Jerusalem?
options: Twenty-nine years
Forty-one years
Fifty-five years
Thirty-one years
explanation: 2 Kings 21:1 records that Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign and reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. Twenty-nine years (wrong_detail) is the length of his father Hezekiah's reign (18:2). Forty-one years (wrong_detail) belongs to his descendant Josiah. Thirty-one years (wrong_detail) is also associated with Josiah's reign (22:1), not Manasseh's.

content: Who succeeded Manasseh as king of Judah immediately after his death?
options: Amon, his son
Josiah, his grandson
Jehoahaz, his son
Jehoiakim, his grandson
explanation: 2 Kings 21:18–19 records that Manasseh slept with his fathers and his son Amon reigned in his place. Josiah (near_passage) was the son of Amon and succeeded Amon—not Manasseh directly. Jehoahaz (wrong_scope) was a later king, the son of Josiah. Jehoiakim (wrong_scope) was also a much later king and did not immediately succeed Manasseh.

content: According to the text, how did the sign the LORD gave Hezekiah to confirm the promise of healing actually occur?
options: The shadow on the sundial of Ahaz went forward ten steps
The sun stood still at noon for one hour
The moon shone brightly in the middle of the day
The shadow on the sundial of Ahaz went back ten steps
explanation: 2 Kings 20:9–11 records that Hezekiah chose to have the shadow go back, and Isaiah prayed so that the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz went back ten steps. The shadow 'going forward ten steps' (wrong_detail) would have been the easier sign and is the exact opposite direction of the true miracle, making it an almost-right answer pointing the wrong way. 'The sun standing still' (common_misconception) is confused with the miracle in the time of Joshua. 'The moon shining brightly' (wrong_detail) does not appear anywhere in this miracle account.

content: After Hezekiah had shown the messengers all his treasuries, what did the prophet Isaiah foretell would happen to those treasures and to the king's descendants?
options: They would be plundered by the Assyrian army during the king's own lifetime
They would be carried away to Babylon, and his descendants would become eunuchs
They would be burned along with the temple immediately
They would be preserved intact until the days of Josiah
explanation: 2 Kings 20:17–18 records that Isaiah prophesied everything in the palace would be carried away to Babylon, and the king's own descendants would be taken to serve as eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. 'The Assyrian army plundering in the king's lifetime' (near_passage) confuses this with the Assyrian threat in chapters 18–19, but the prophecy points specifically to Babylon and to future generations. 'Burned immediately' (wrong_detail) is wrong about both the timing and the manner. 'Preserved until the days of Josiah' (true_but_off) directly contradicts the content of the warning.

content: Why does Hezekiah's response to Isaiah's prophecy about the Babylonian disaster reveal that he was thinking primarily about his own lifetime?
options: Because he was glad that there would be peace and security in his own days
Because he asked the LORD to withdraw the prophecy of disaster
Because he immediately called the people to repent and tear their garments
Because he ordered the Babylonian messengers to be sent away at once
explanation: 2 Kings 20:19 records that Hezekiah replied, 'The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good,' and thought to himself, 'There will be peace and security in my days,' showing he was at ease because the disaster would fall on future generations, not his own. 'Asking the LORD to withdraw the prophecy' (wrong_detail) did not happen; he accepted the word without protest. 'Calling the people to repent and tear their garments' (common_misconception) confuses his reaction with that of other kings who responded to pronouncements of disaster with public mourning. 'Sending the messengers away immediately' (wrong_detail) did not occur; he had already received them and displayed all his treasures to them.

content: What evil practices of Manasseh does the text specifically list as provoking the LORD's anger?
options: Setting up a golden calf and worshipping it at Bethel
Offering his daughter as a burnt offering to Dagon
Making his son pass through fire, practicing divination, and consulting mediums and sorcerers
Plundering the temple to build a shrine to Ashtoreth
explanation: 2 Kings 21:6 records that Manasseh burned his son as an offering, practiced fortune-telling, used sorcery, and consulted mediums and necromancers. 'A golden calf at Bethel' (near_passage) was the sin of Jeroboam recorded in 1 Kings, not Manasseh. 'Offering his daughter to Dagon' (wrong_detail) is wrong about both the person offered and the deity involved. 'Building a shrine to Ashtoreth' (wrong_detail) confuses Manasseh's sins with those of Solomon in an earlier era, and is not among the acts recorded here about Manasseh.

content: When the prophets pronounced disaster on Jerusalem because of Manasseh's sins, what images from the past did they invoke to describe the coming judgment?
options: The sulfur fire of Sodom and the flood of Noah
The measuring line of Samaria and the plumb line of the house of Ahab
The plagues of Egypt and the sword of the Amalekites
The Babylonian yoke and seventy years of exile
explanation: 2 Kings 21:13 records the LORD declaring He would stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria and the plumb line of the house of Ahab, applying the same standard of judgment that destroyed those before. 'Sodom and Noah' (common_misconception) are familiar symbols of divine judgment but are not the images this passage uses. 'The plagues of Egypt and the Amalekites' (wrong_detail) belong to the Exodus era and are unrelated to the pronouncement of judgment here. 'The Babylonian yoke of seventy years' (true_but_off) is what was ultimately fulfilled, but it is not the comparative image the prophets invoke in this particular verse.

content: In what essential way did the transfer of power following King Amon's death differ from an ordinary coup?
options: The conspirators seized the throne and established a new dynasty
A foreign king appointed a trusted ally to rule in Amon's place
The priests chose someone outside the royal family to be king
The people of the land killed the conspirators and crowned the king's son
explanation: 2 Kings 21:23–24 records that Amon's servants conspired and killed the king, but then the people of the land killed all the conspirators and made Josiah, the king's son, king in his place, thereby preserving the Davidic line. 'The conspirators seizing the throne and founding a new dynasty' (wrong_detail) is precisely the opposite of what happened: the conspirators were themselves executed. 'A foreign king appointing a ruler' (wrong_scope) describes a different kind of succession that occurred with later kings in Judah's history. 'The priests choosing someone outside the royal family' (common_misconception) confuses this event with Jehoiada's crowning of Joash in an earlier episode, and even in that case the one crowned was still of the royal bloodline.

content: According to 2 Kings 22, how old was Josiah when he became king of Judah?
options: Eight years old
Twelve years old
Sixteen years old
Twenty-five years old
explanation: 2 Kings 22:1 states: 'Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem' → the correct answer is 'Eight years old.' 'Twelve years old' gives the wrong number (wrong_detail). 'Sixteen years old' is also the wrong number, close to the age at which Josiah began to seek God according to 2 Chronicles 34:3 (near_passage). 'Twenty-five years old' is the age at which some other kings of Judah became king, not Josiah (wrong_detail).

content: When King Josiah sent messengers to inquire of the LORD regarding the words in the book of the law, which prophetess did they go to see?
options: Deborah
Huldah
Miriam
Anna
explanation: 2 Kings 22:14 records that the king's messengers 'went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum... dwelling in Jerusalem' → the correct answer is 'Huldah.' 'Deborah' was a prophetess in the time of the Judges and does not belong to this passage (wrong_scope). 'Miriam' was a prophetess in the time of the Exodus (wrong_scope). 'Anna' was a prophetess in the New Testament who met Jesus when he was presented at the temple (wrong_scope).

content: According to 2 Kings 22, which high priest found the book of the law in the temple?
options: Shaphan
Abiathar
Hilkiah
Zadok
explanation: 2 Kings 22:8 states: 'Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD"' → the correct answer is 'Hilkiah.' 'Shaphan' was the secretary who received the book and read it to the king, not the one who found it (true_but_off). 'Abiathar' was a priest in the time of King David (wrong_scope). 'Zadok' was also a priest in the time of David and Solomon and does not belong to this passage (wrong_scope).

content: According to 2 Kings 23, where did King Josiah die in battle when he went out to meet the king of Egypt?
options: Megiddo
Gilgal
Bethel
Gibeon
explanation: 2 Kings 23:29 records that Pharaoh Neco went up... 'King Josiah went to meet him, and Pharaoh Neco killed him at Megiddo as soon as he saw him' → the correct answer is 'Megiddo.' 'Gilgal' was where the Israelites camped in the time of Joshua (wrong_scope). 'Bethel' is where Josiah destroyed the altar in the same chapter 23, but it is not where the king died (near_passage). 'Gibeon' is where Solomon had his dream encounter with the LORD and is unrelated to this passage (wrong_scope).

content: The prophetess Huldah foretold that disaster would come upon Jerusalem, but what did she promise Josiah specifically because his heart was tender and he humbled himself before the LORD?
options: He would be gathered to his grave in peace and his eyes would not see the disaster that would come
He would defeat all his enemies and reign until he was a hundred years old
He would be taken to another land before the city was destroyed
He would see the city restored in his own lifetime
explanation: 2 Kings 22:20 records the LORD speaking through Huldah: 'I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place' → the correct answer. The promise was that the king would die before the disaster, not that he would live long or be victorious: 'He would defeat all his enemies and reign until he was a hundred years old' mischaracterizes the nature of the reward according to the text (wrong_detail), and Josiah in fact died in battle at Megiddo (true_but_off, cf. 23:29). 'He would be taken to another land' describes a different means of escape than the actual promise (wrong_detail). 'He would see the city restored' contradicts the very words of the promise — 'your eyes shall not see all the disaster' — the promise is that he would not witness the destruction, not that he would witness a restoration (wrong_detail).

content: According to the text, after bringing out the vessels made for Baal and Asherah from the temple and burning them, what did Josiah do with their ashes to express the utmost defilement?
options: Scattered them on the graves of the common people
Poured them into the Kidron Valley and scattered them at Bethel
Poured them into the spring of Gihon outside the city
Buried them at the foot of the walls of Jerusalem
explanation: 2 Kings 23:6 (ESV) records that the king 'brought out the Asherah from the house of the LORD, outside Jerusalem, to the Kidron Valley, and burned it at the Kidron Valley and beat it to dust and cast the dust of it upon the graves of the common people'; and verse 4 records that the ashes of the vessels for Baal were carried 'to Bethel.' The answer 'Poured into the Kidron Valley and scattered at Bethel' correctly combines both locations mentioned in the text. 'Scattered on the graves of the common people' is partially correct (the graves of the common people appear in verse 6) but omits and misplaces the primary location, making it almost-right (true_but_off). 'Poured into the spring of Gihon' substitutes the Kidron Valley with a different water source in Jerusalem (wrong_detail). 'Buried at the foot of the city walls' describes an action not found in the text (wrong_detail).

content: What does the text emphasize as the reason the Passover that Josiah commanded was particularly remarkable?
options: It was the first time the people had kept the feast since coming out of Egypt
No such Passover had been kept since the days of the judges until that time
It was the only Passover celebrated outside Jerusalem
The feast lasted twice as many days as the law prescribed
explanation: 2 Kings 23:22 (ESV) records: 'For no such Passover had been kept since the days of the judges who judged Israel, or during all the days of the kings of Israel or of the kings of Judah' → the correct answer captures the unprecedented nature of the feast since the days of the judges. 'The first time since coming out of Egypt' overstates the timeframe, since the people had observed this feast many times in the intervening centuries (wrong_detail). 'Celebrated outside Jerusalem' contradicts the text, which states the feast was kept in Jerusalem (wrong_detail). 'Lasted twice as many days' is a fabricated detail not found anywhere in the passage (wrong_detail).

content: When Josiah destroyed the altar at Bethel, he had bones taken from the tombs and burned on the altar; but he commanded that one tomb be left undisturbed. Whose tomb was it?
options: The tomb of the man of God from Judah who had prophesied these things
The tomb of the prophet Elijah, who boldly stood against the wicked king Ahab
The tomb of the patriarch Jacob, who once dreamed of a ladder at Bethel
The tomb of King Jeroboam, who had set up the altar with the golden calf at Bethel
explanation: 2 Kings 23:17–18 (ESV) records that when the king saw the tomb he asked about it, and the men of the city told him, 'It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and predicted these things that you have done against the altar at Bethel,' so the king commanded: 'Leave him alone; let no man move his bones' → this is the correct answer. 'The tomb of the prophet Elijah' names the wrong person, since Elijah was taken up to heaven and has no earthly tomb (common_misconception). 'The tomb of the patriarch Jacob' links Bethel to Jacob's story in Genesis but has no connection to this passage (wrong_scope). 'The tomb of King Jeroboam' refers to the one who established the Bethel altar and was condemned, not the tomb that was spared (true_but_off).

content: Despite praising Josiah in the highest terms, the text reveals that the LORD's fierce anger against Judah did not turn away. According to this passage, what was the core reason disaster was still destined to fall?
options: Because of the sins of Manasseh, who had provoked the LORD to anger
Because Josiah himself sinned in his later years
Because the people refused to keep the covenant the king had just established
Because the priests at the high places were still offering sacrifices to other gods
explanation: 2 Kings 23:26 (ESV) records: 'Still the LORD did not turn from the burning of his great wrath, by which his anger was kindled against Judah, because of all the provocations with which Manasseh had provoked him' → the cause was the sins of the previous king Manasseh, not any fault of Josiah or the people of that day. 'Because Josiah himself sinned in his later years' contradicts verse 25, which praises the king for turning to the LORD with all his heart above all the kings of Judah (wrong_detail, almost-right since it echoes the motif of a king falling in old age as Solomon did). 'Because the people refused to keep the covenant' contradicts verse 3, which shows the whole people pledged themselves to the covenant (wrong_detail, almost-right because it connects to the covenant ceremony in the same chapter). 'Because the priests at the high places were still offering sacrifices' describes something Josiah had already abolished in the same chapter and is therefore no longer a valid cause (true_but_off).

content: Josiah defiled the high places east of Jerusalem that the text explicitly attributes to a previous king who had built them for foreign gods. Who was that previous king?
options: Solomon
Ahaz
Manasseh
Jeroboam
explanation: 2 Kings 23:13 (ESV) records that the king defiled 'the high places that were to the east of Jerusalem... which Solomon the king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites' → the correct answer is Solomon, who built these high places for the gods of his foreign wives (cf. 1 Kings 11:7). 'Ahaz' had erected foreign altars inside the temple (2 Kings 16), making him a plausible choice, but he is not the builder of these particular high places (true_but_off, almost-right). 'Manasseh' built numerous high places and is heavily condemned elsewhere in the same book, making confusion easy, but verse 13 names Solomon explicitly (true_but_off, almost-right). 'Jeroboam' set up altars at Bethel and Dan in the northern kingdom, not the high places east of Jerusalem (wrong_scope).

content: How old was King Jehoiachin when he began to reign over Judah?
options: Eighteen years old
Twenty-one years old
Twenty-five years old
Eight years old
explanation: According to 2 Kings 24:8, 'Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king.' (wrong_detail) 'Twenty-one years old' was the age of Zedekiah when he began to reign (24:18), not Jehoiachin. (wrong_detail) 'Twenty-five years old' does not match the age of any king in this passage. (common_misconception) 'Eight years old' is confused with Josiah, who became king at age eight in an earlier chapter, outside the scope of chapters 24–25.

content: How long did King Jehoiachin of Judah reign in Jerusalem before being taken into captivity?
options: Three months
Eleven years
Three years
Forty years
explanation: According to 2 Kings 24:8, Jehoiachin 'reigned three months in Jerusalem.' (wrong_detail) 'Eleven years' was the length of Zedekiah's reign (24:18). (near_passage) 'Three years' was how long Jehoiakim served Nebuchadnezzar before rebelling (24:1), referring to a different king. (common_misconception) 'Forty years' evokes the reigns of David or Solomon and has no connection to this passage.

content: After installing Mattaniah as a puppet king in Judah, what name did the king of Babylon give him?
options: Zedekiah
Jehoiachin
Gedaliah
Eliakim
explanation: According to 2 Kings 24:17, the king of Babylon 'made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah.' (wrong_scope) 'Jehoiachin' was the king who was taken captive — the one Mattaniah replaced — not a new name given to Mattaniah. (near_passage) 'Gedaliah' was the governor appointed after the fall of Jerusalem (25:22), not a king. (wrong_detail) 'Eliakim' was the former name of Jehoiakim, which was changed in an earlier passage outside the scope of chapters 24–25.

content: After being captured by the Babylonian army, what physical punishment did King Zedekiah suffer before being led away to Babylon?
options: His eyes were put out
His hands were cut off
His tongue was cut out
He was burned alive
explanation: According to 2 Kings 25:7, they 'put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains of bronze and took him to Babylon.' (wrong_detail) 'His hands were cut off' is not the punishment recorded; he was bound in chains, not mutilated in that way. (wrong_detail) 'His tongue was cut out' does not appear in the text. (wrong_detail) 'He was burned alive' confuses the burning of the temple and the palace (25:9) with what was done to the king himself.

content: When Jerusalem's walls were breached, King Zedekiah attempted to flee but was overtaken and captured by the Chaldean army at what location?
options: In the plains of Jericho
On the Mount of Olives
At the city of Riblah
At the Euphrates River
explanation: According to 2 Kings 25:5, 'the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook him in the plains of Jericho.' (wrong_detail) 'On the Mount of Olives' is the direction toward which the king fled but is not the place where he was captured — close in geography but wrong in the specific detail of location. (near_passage) 'At the city of Riblah' is where Zedekiah was brought to stand trial after his capture (25:6), not the site of the capture itself. (wrong_scope) 'At the Euphrates River' is not mentioned as the place where the king was caught in this passage.

content: What did Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, do to Jerusalem after capturing it?
options: Burned the temple, the king's palace, and broke down the walls of the city
Left the temple intact but destroyed the king's palace
Only broke down the walls, keeping the temple
Built the city into a fortress for Gedaliah
explanation: According to 2 Kings 25:9-10, Nebuzaradan 'burned the house of the LORD and the king's house' and 'broke down the walls around Jerusalem.' (wrong_detail) 'Left the temple intact but destroyed the king's palace' is wrong because the temple was also burned — only half correct. (wrong_detail) 'Only broke down the walls, keeping the temple' is wrong because the temple was burned — close but missing a key detail. (wrong_scope) 'Built the city into a fortress for Gedaliah' reverses the truth: the city was destroyed, and Gedaliah was merely appointed governor over the remaining people.

content: Why was Gedaliah, who was appointed governor over the remaining people of Judah, killed?
options: He was assassinated by Ishmael, a man of royal descent, along with those who were with him
He was publicly executed by Babylonian troops for plotting rebellion against the empire
The people of the city stoned him to death in anger over the sin of idolatry
He died of famine along with the people of the city while Jerusalem was besieged by the enemy
explanation: According to 2 Kings 25:25, 'Ishmael... of the royal family, came with ten men and struck down Gedaliah,' along with the Jews and Chaldeans who were with him. (wrong_detail) 'Executed by Babylonian troops' is wrong because the Babylonians had appointed him; he was killed by a Judahite. (wrong_scope) 'Stoned by the people for idolatry' is not in the text — this attributes a false reason. (near_passage) 'Died of famine' confuses this event with the famine during the siege (25:3), which is unrelated to Gedaliah's death.

content: At the end of 2 Kings, which king of Babylon released Jehoiachin from prison and granted him a position of honor?
options: Evil-merodach
Nebuchadnezzar
Belshazzar
Cyrus the Persian
explanation: According to 2 Kings 25:27, 'Evil-merodach king of Babylon... graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison' and gave him a seat above the other captive kings. (near_passage) 'Nebuchadnezzar' was the king who captured and imprisoned Jehoiachin (24:12-15), not the one who freed him. (wrong_scope) 'Belshazzar' appears in the book of Daniel, which is outside the scope of 2 Kings. (wrong_scope) 'Cyrus the Persian' is associated with the return of the Judean exiles in Chronicles and Ezra, not this passage.

content: According to the narrative, what is the deep theological reason why the LORD removed Judah and brought disaster upon it, beyond the political rebellions of its kings?
options: Because of the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed, which the LORD was not willing to pardon
Because King Jehoiakim had stopped paying tribute to the Babylonian empire for three years
Because the people of the land collectively refused to pay the temple tax in Jerusalem
Because King Zedekiah secretly allied with Egypt to resist the mighty Babylonian empire
explanation: According to 2 Kings 24:3-4, disaster came upon Judah 'because of the sins of Manasseh... and also for the innocent blood that he had shed... the LORD was not willing to pardon.' This is the root theological cause. (near_passage) 'Jehoiakim stopped paying tribute' (24:1) is the immediate political trigger — factually accurate but not the deep theological reason the question asks for. (wrong_scope) 'The people refused to pay the temple tax' is not found in the text. (true_but_off) 'Zedekiah's alliance with Egypt' reflects historical context but is not the reason stated in 24:3-4.

content: Comparing the recorded timestamps, which event occurred FIRST in the sequence of Jerusalem's fall?
options: The Babylonian army began besieging the city in the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign
Nebuzaradan burned the temple in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign
The walls of Jerusalem were broken down all around
Zedekiah had his eyes gouged out and was taken to Babylon
explanation: According to 2 Kings 25:1, the siege began 'in the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month' — this is the earliest event in the sequence. The city was breached in the eleventh year (25:2-3), then the king was captured and blinded (25:7), and afterward the temple was burned 'in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar' (25:8). (true_but_off) 'Nebuzaradan burned the temple' is a real event but occurred AFTER the city had already fallen, in the fifth month. (wrong_detail) 'The walls were broken down' (25:10) occurred in the same campaign as the burning — after the siege had ended. (true_but_off) 'Zedekiah had his eyes gouged out' (25:7) happened after the city fell, not before the siege began.
